title: Faith in mind
hookLine: a Chan poem attributed to the third patriarch Sengcan: the great way is not hard for those without picking and choosing

lines: THE GREAT WAY IS NOT DIFFICULT.
cards: The great way is not difficult. That's how the poem opens, and for half a line it sounds like very good news. Then comes the condition: it is not difficult for those who don't pick and choose.
Which can describe a whole morning. Coffee or tea. Skip this song.
That email can wait, this one can't. The poem is short and plain, built from paired lines that sound almost like proverbs, and some Chan and Zen students chant it and carry it.
Tradition credits it to Sengcan, remembered in the Chan lineage as the third ancestor, counting Bodhidharma as the first.

teach.b: In Chinese the title is Xinxin Ming, often given in English as Faith in Mind, or Trust in Mind. The two words read xin are different. The first means trust or faith.
The second means heart-mind, the whole of what thinks and feels. So this faith isn't faith in a creed. Some readers hear it as trust that the mind, as it is, is already enough to meet the way.
In paraphrase, the poem goes on: when love and hate are both absent, everything becomes clear and open.
The way isn't hidden. Something stands in front of it, and the poem names it: the habit of grabbing at one side and pushing away the other.

teach.h: TASTE IS FINE; THE WAR IS NOT.
teach.b: That doesn't mean stop having taste. You can still notice that the tea is too strong.
What the poem calls the sickness of the mind is setting what you like against what you dislike, turning every small preference into a quiet war. Rain on the day of a picnic is rain.
The poem's interest is in everything piled on top of the rain. And why faith?
The poem describes the way as round and complete, like vast space, with nothing lacking and nothing extra.

Only taking and rejecting, it says, keeps it from being seen so. Yesterday's just sitting is this same trust done with the body: no target, no improvement project. The poem puts that trust into words.

how: In some Zen and Chan communities the Xinxin Ming is chanted or recited in services and studied in talks, and students often learn its opening lines by heart.

games.q: it rains on the day you planned a picnic, and the poem's first line comes to mind. what is the poem pointing at?
o: the rain, and the fight piled on top of it
pretend you wanted rain all along
games.why: the poem doesn't ask you to fake a preference. it points at the war between liking and disliking, the thing piled on top of the rain.

practice: For this sit, take what the body brings, an itch on the cheek, a stiff knee, cool air on the hands, each with an urge attached to scratch, shift or fix it.
You don't need to obey the urge or fight it; see it as a preference, and let the sensation be a sensation for a few breaths. If you do need to move, move slowly, knowing you chose.

wordCard.voice: Xinxin Ming. The Chan poem whose title is often rendered Faith in Mind, and which opens: the great way is not difficult for those who don't pick and choose. Today's word.
